newsitem.title: BULGARIA: NEW BULGARIAN PRESIDENT INHERITS POLITICAL DEADLOCK.
newsitem.headline: NEW BULGARIAN PRESIDENT INHERITS POLITICAL DEADLOCK.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president Petar Stoyanov formally takes office on Wednesday, inheriting political deadlock that has blocked formation of a new government to haul the country back from economic collapse.

Stoyanov, who was elected last November and took the oath of office last Sunday, will receive the key to the presidency from outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev, the first democratically elected head of state in Bulgaria's 13 century history.

Stoyanov has already begun mediation efforts and both government and opposition hope the 44-year-old divorce lawyer can break the deadlock over formation of a new cabinet and the date for a general election.

At his inauguration on Sunday, Stoyanov backed opposition calls for a quick election to restore confidence in government and put an end to daily street protests, which enter their 16th day on Wednesday.

The Socialists have offered elections in December, a year ahead of schedule, but want to form a second cabinet following the resignation of prime minister Zhan Videnov on December 21. The UDF wants elections in March.
Videnov urged Stoyanov to hand the mandate to the Socialists' nominee for premier, Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, saying he had a programme ready to bring the country out of crisis.

"In the next few days the new president faces the choice either to hand the mandate to a government which will be mandated to hold negotiations with international lending institutions...or the choice of holding elections in conditions of hyperinflation," Videnov said on Tuesday.
The opposition blames Videnov for leading the country to the verge of default on its $10 billion foreign debt.

The opposition has held 15 consecutive days of protests for immediate elections and against a second Socialist cabinet, and besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10 after the Socialists refused to vote on their proposal.
Stoyanov met the resident European Union and International Monetary Fund representatives on Tuesday to discuss prospects for external funding.
In his final address to the nation as president, Zhelev laid the blame on the country's ex-communist rulers, and on the constitution, which places most power in the hands of parliament.
"Bulgaria's model of transition failed because for seven years economic and social reforms were not carried out. Instead of coming out of the crisis, Bulgaria is sinking lower," he said.

Government corruption and resistance to reform have left Bulgaria lagging behind other eastern European states. Annual inflation is running at more than 300 percent and a flight into dollars has pushed the lev to a new all-time low on Tuesday of 760 to the dollar from about 70 a year ago.

Zhelev, a dissident philosopher and one of the key figures in Bulgaria's transition from one-party rule, lost a U.S.-style primary to Stoyanov last June, and Stoyanov ran as the opposition candidate in last November's election, defeating the Socialist candidate in the second round.
Zhelev, who last year founded a new political party, said he would work in his retirement for the expansion of the president's powers.

On Tuesday, as doctors, students and Gypsies joined the daily rally outside Sofia's gold-domed Orthodox cathedral, the Socialists warned they were under pressure from regional party groups to organise pro-government counter-rallies.
"They insist that we must have a tougher approach against the pressure of the opposition," said Vassil Karinov, a member of the Socialists' executive bureau.
Counter-rallies by supporters of neighbouring Serbia's Socialist President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade on December 24 led to violent clashes between demonstrators and police.
One-hour warning strikes took place in several factories and mines around the country on Tuesday. Unions threaten full-scale strikes if the opposition's demands are not met.
